1781-1800

Caption This

Creating the Constitution

4

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

A wagon pulled two ways

Not done

What you’re looking at: A hand-colored print from Norton Ch. 6. A big wagon marked “Connecticut” sits in the middle. Two groups of men in old-fashioned coats pull it in opposite directions with chains. A man sits on top of the load and waves a sword. At the bottom, a line says Connecticut pays an impost (a tax on goods) to New York.

  • Look at the two groups pulling the wagon. What happens to a wagon when two teams pull opposite ways?
  • Under the Articles, each state mostly acted on its own. How could that cause trouble over taxes and trade?

Image 2 of 5

The Constitutional Convention

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color painting from Norton Ch. 6. A large crowd of men in 1700s coats, stockings, and powdered hair fills a big hall. Some sit and talk in small groups. Others stand around a table in the middle where a man bends over papers. A man sits on a raised platform at the right. This is how artists have pictured the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia.

Heads up: This was a serious meeting, and its choices about slavery and women's rights hurt many people. Aim your joke at the crowded room, the heavy coats, or how long meetings last. Never joke about enslaved people or women's rights.

  • Count how many people are in the room. Why might it be hard to agree on anything?
  • The delegates had to settle fights between large states and small states. How might a compromise help?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 3 of 5

A busy print shop

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white woodcut from Norton Ch. 6. Four people work in a small shop. A big wooden printing press stands on the right. On the left, one person taps a block of letters with a small mallet. Another works at a slanted stand of letters. A third lifts a large frame, and a fourth inks the letters with two round pads. Small numbers mark the parts of the shop.

Heads up: Some of the workers look young. Aim your joke at the ink, the noise, the deadlines, or the big wooden press. Never joke about the people at work.

  • Look at the big press and the table of letters. How slow would it be to print one newspaper this way?
  • Norton says The Federalist Papers ran in New York newspapers. Why would printed essays matter in a big argument?

Image 4 of 5

A fight in the legislature

Not done

What you’re looking at: A hand-colored print from Norton Ch. 6. Two men with wild hair swing a cane and a pair of fire tongs at each other in a crowded room. Men all around shout, wave hats, and watch. One man sits in a chair and laughs. The faces are drawn in an exaggerated, cartoon way. It is a print of a real fight between two members of Congress in 1798.

Heads up: This is a cartoon-style print of a real fight between politicians. Aim your joke at the brawl, the cane and the tongs, or leaders who cannot agree. Never joke about how anyone looks.

  • Look at the cane and the fire tongs. What does this tell you about how heated politics was in the 1790s?
  • Norton calls the 1790s an “age of passion.” What were Federalists and Republicans fighting about?

Image 5 of 5

Burning a Jay effigy

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colored print from Norton Ch. 6. A crowd of men gathers at night around a fire. Some hold torches and sticks. A large dummy, called an effigy, hangs above the smoke with the word “JAY” on its vest. This is a protest, and the dummy is not a real person.

Heads up: This is a protest where a dummy, not a person, is burned. Aim your joke at the torches, the fire, or an angry crowd that argues about a treaty. Never joke about hurting a real person.

  • Look at the torches and the crowd. How do you think these people felt about the treaty?
  • Jay agreed to some British demands. Why might Americans who liked France be angry?
